title: Jungle Animals
strapline: Stripes, spots and swinging through the canopy — the wildest classroom, from the forest floor up.
intent: Meet animals utterly unlike the ones outside our window — and the words that come with them: camouflage, predator, canopy, nocturnal.
Explore pattern where nature shows off: tiger stripes, leopard spots, snake scales — spot it, sort by it, print it.
Compare boldly: the elephant is heavier than everything, the snake is longer than the carpet, the tree frog is smaller than your thumb.
Move like the animals move — slither, swing, prowl, stampede — bringing the jungle into children's whole bodies.
Grow respect for wild creatures and their far-away homes: real animals live in real jungles, and they deserve looking after.
implementation: Layer the habitat properly — forest floor, understorey, canopy — with plants, logs and draped greenery, and talk about who lives at each level.
Introduce camouflage as a game: hide the patterned animals against matching fabrics and hunt for them together.
Model the rich vocabulary while children play — 'the leopard's spots are her camouflage; she's almost invisible in the leaves'.
Take the animals large: an animal-walk trail outside where everyone slithers, prowls, swings and stampedes in turn.
Pair figures with the room's jungle stories, then leave the props out for retelling with new endings.
Compare the jungle's weather with ours out the window: it rains there nearly every day — hotter rain than ours.
Talk about jungles as real, precious places where these animals genuinely live — not just a story-land.
key_questions: Why do you think the tiger has stripes and the leopard has spots?
Who lives at the top of the trees, and who stays down on the forest floor?
Which animal would you hear first at night in the jungle?
How is the jungle's weather different from ours today?
Where should the baby elephant hide when the tiger prowls past?

impact.text: Children move like the animals with control — slithering low, prowling slowly, swinging arm over arm, stampeding without collisions.
Children use jungle vocabulary precisely — camouflage, predator, canopy, nocturnal — and explain the words to friends.
Children sort and match animals by pattern — striped, spotted, scaly — and continue the patterns in printing and painting.
Children compare the animals — the elephant is the heaviest, the snake is longer than the whole carpet — reaching for comparing words as they play.
Children retell the room's jungle stories with the figures as props, inventing their own variations on the ending.
Children talk about the jungle's hot, rainy weather and compare it with what's outside our own window today.
Children treat the creatures — plastic and real — gently, and talk about jungles as real homes that need protecting.
Children build sustained jungle narratives together — the watering hole at dusk, the lost cub, the tiger on the prowl — sharing out the roles.

enhancements: Draped green fabric, pot plants and cardboard-tube trees to build a true canopy layer above the play.
A camouflage hunt: patterned animals hidden against matching patterned fabrics — who can spot the leopard?
Animal-print blocks and paint for making stripe and spot patterns, then matching them back to their owners.
A muddy watering hole (cocoa dough or wet clay) where every animal comes down to drink at dusk.
Jungle sounds played low during play — rain, birds, a distant roar — and a guessing game to name each call.
String for measuring: lay out a real python's length down the corridor and count how many children long it is.
Binoculars, a safari hat and a wildlife-spotter's checklist for recording who was seen at the watering hole.

playing_exploring: The layered habitat invites exploration up and down — who's hiding under the log, who's up in the leaves?
Children throw their whole bodies into being the animals, feeling each way of moving from the inside.
active_learning: The camouflage hunt rewards slow, careful looking — the leopard only appears to children who keep trying.
Children work at their stripe patterns until they genuinely repeat, checking against the tiger.
creating_thinking: Children reason about why animals look the way they do, building their own camouflage theory.
Weaving separate animals into one watering-hole story — who drinks, who hides, who prowls — is thinking made visible.
